lmsArticle.title: LLD for URL Shortener: Designing TinyURL
lmsArticle.subtitle: How do you turn a long URL into a 7-character string? We explore Base62 encoding, Hash collisions, and database choices.
lmsArticle.excerpt:
TLDR

TLDR: A URL Shortener maps long URLs to short IDs. The core challenge is generating a globally unique, short, collision-free ID at scale. We use Base62 encoding on auto-incrementing database IDs
lmsArticle.content:
## Scenario context

```architecture
{
  "version": 1,
  "title": "URL Shortener Architecture - Range Allocation & Read-Path Caching",
  "description": "High-throughput redirection architecture combining ZooKeeper range-based ticket allocation with aggressive Redis read caching.",
  "view": "high-level",
  "pattern": "cache-aside",
  "direction": "LR",
  "groups": [
    { "id": "ingress", "label": "Edge Ingress", "tone": "slate" },…

This walkthrough focuses on **Why Base62 and Not MD5?**.

Before making a design choice, clarify:

- Approach A — Hashing (MD5/SHA): - Hash the long URL: MD5("https://...") = 3b94d2a8...
- - Take first 7 chars: 3b94d2a .
- - Problem: Two different URLs might produce the same first 7 chars → collision → wrong redirect.

**Concepts in play:** caching, design-patterns-gof, jvm-internals-and-garbage-collection, low-level-design-systems

## Stage 1 — The Locker Room Analogy

- A locker room assigns locker numbers.
- The attendant doesn't randomly pick numbers — she uses the next available sequential number.
- You get "Locker 5" → you can find it instantly.
- URL shorteners work the same way: assign a unique sequential integer ID , then encode it in a compact string format.

*Applies **caching** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** URL shorteners work the same way: assign a unique sequential integer ID , then encode it in a compact string format.

## Stage 2 — Short Codes, Redirects, and TTL: The Core Vocabulary

- Before building, align on the four concepts everything else depends on.
- Short Code — the compact identifier that replaces a long URL.
- cb , Xk3 , and my-blog are all short codes.
- They appear after the domain: https://tiny.url/cb .

*Applies **design-patterns-gof** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** They appear after the domain: https://tiny.url/cb .

## Stage 3 — OOP Contracts: Interfaces and Collaborations

- The URL shortener's backbone is four focused Java interfaces.
- Each defines a contract — an agreement about what a collaborator can do without revealing how it does it.
- UrlShortenerService holds a reference to each interface and receives them via constructor injection; it never references a concrete class directly.
- Who implements each interface, who calls it, and what it abstracts: Runtime collaboration — how the components interact during a shorten() call: Structural relationships — ownership and implementation: This class diagra…

*Applies **jvm-internals-and-garbage-collection** to the decision above.*

```java
interface UrlEncoder {
    String encode(long id);  // converts counter ID to Base62 short code
}

interface CodeStore {
    String save(String longUrl);            // stores mapping, returns short code
    Optional<String> resolve(String code);  // looks up long URL by short code
    boolean exists(String code);            // deduplication check
}

interface AnalyticsTracker {
    void recordClick(String code, String referrer, Instant timestamp);
}

interface AliasValidator {
    boolean isValid(String customAlias);    // checks format, uniqueness, reserved words
}
```

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Client -->|"shorten(longUrl)"| SVC[UrlShortenerService]
    SVC -->|"save(longUrl)"| Store["CodeStore (RedisStore / InMemoryStore)"]
    Store -->|shortCode| SVC
    SVC -->|"encode(id)"| Encoder["UrlEncoder (Base62Encoder)"]
    Encoder -->|"cb"| SVC
    SVC -->|shortCode| Client
```

**Observable outcome:** Who implements each interface, who calls it, and what it abstracts: Runtime collaboration — how the components interact during a shorten() call: Structural relationships — ownership and implementation: This class diagra…

## Stage 4 — OOP Pillars Applied to the URL Shortener

- Each classical OOP pillar maps directly to a concrete design decision in this system.
- Encapsulation — Base62Encoder owns its alphabet The 62-character alphabet ( a-z A-Z 0-9 ) and the modular-arithmetic encoding loop are private implementation details inside Base62Encoder .
- Callers invoke encode(125) and receive "cb" — they never see the CHARS constant or the while (id 0) loop.
- Swapping the alphabet (say, to a URL-safe Base64 variant) requires editing exactly one class, nowhere else.

*Applies **low-level-design-systems** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** Swapping the alphabet (say, to a URL-safe Base64 variant) requires editing exactly one class, nowhere else.

## Stage 5 — SOLID Principles in the URL Shortener Design

- SOLID is not an abstract checklist — each principle appears as a specific, verifiable choice here.
- Single Responsibility (SRP) — Each class has exactly one reason to change.
- Base62Encoder changes only if the encoding algorithm changes.
- A CodeStore implementation changes only if the persistence technology changes.

*Applies **caching** to the decision above.*

```java
public class UrlShortenerService {
    private final UrlEncoder encoder;
    private final CodeStore store;
    private final AnalyticsTracker tracker;

    public UrlShortenerService(UrlEncoder encoder, CodeStore store, AnalyticsTracker tracker) {
        this.encoder = encoder;
        this.store   = store;
        this.tracker = tracker;
    }
}
```

**Observable outcome:** A CodeStore implementation changes only if the persistence technology changes.

## Stage 6 — Interface Contracts: The Four Boundaries of the URL Shortener

- Each interface is a stable boundary.
- Anything inside that boundary can change freely; anything outside can only call the methods listed here.
- These four contracts are everything UrlShortenerService needs from the outside world.
- Any Spring @Bean that satisfies an interface can be wired in — production configs, test configs, and migration configs all swap implementations without modifying the service itself.

*Applies **design-patterns-gof** to the decision above.*

```java
/**
 * Converts a numeric counter ID into a compact short-code string.
 * Implementations: Base62Encoder, CustomAliasEncoder, Base58Encoder
 */
interface UrlEncoder {
    String encode(long id);  // e.g. encode(125) → "cb"
}

/**
 * Persists and retrieves short-code ↔ long-URL mappings.
 * Implementations: InMemoryStore (test), RedisStore (staging), DistributedStore (prod)
 */
interface CodeStore {
    String save(String longUrl);            // persists mapping, returns generated short code
    Optional<String> resolve(String code);  // returns long URL for code, or empty if not found
    boolean exists(String code);            // returns true if the code is already in use
}

/**
 * Records analytics for every redirect event.
 * Implementations: NoOpTracker (default), DatabaseTracker (analytics-on)
 */
interface AnalyticsTracker {
    void recordClick(String code, String referrer, Instant timestamp);
}

/**
 * Validates user-supplied custom aliases before storage.
 * Implementations: CustomAliasValidator
 */
interface AliasValidator {
    boolean isValid(String customAlias);  // false if blank, reserved, non-alphanumeric, or taken
}
```

```mermaid
classDiagram
    class UrlEncoder {
        <<interface>>
        +encode(id long) String
        +decode(code String) long
    }
    class CodeStore {
        <<interface>>
        +save(longUrl String) String
        +resolve(code String) Optional~String~
        +exists(code String) boolean
    }
    class AnalyticsTracker {
        <<interface>>
        +recordClick(code String, referrer String, ts Instant) void
    }
    class AliasValidator {
        <<interface>>
        +isValid(customAlias String) boolean
    }
    class Base62Encoder {
        -String CHARS
        +encode(id long) String
        +decode(code String) long
    }
    class CustomAliasEncoder {
        +encode(id long) String
    }
    class InMemoryStore {
        -Map~String,String~ store
        +save(longUrl String) String
        +resolve(code String) Optional~String~
        +exists(code String) boolean
    }
    class RedisStore {
        +save(longUrl String) String
        +resolve(code String) Optional~String~
        +exists(code String) boolean
    }
    class NoOpTracker {
        +recordClick(code, referrer, ts) void
    }
    class DatabaseTracker {
        +recordClick(code, referrer, ts) void
    }
    class CustomAliasValidator {
        +isValid(customAlias String) boolean
    }
    class UrlShortenerService {
        -UrlEncoder encoder
        -CodeStore store
        -AnalyticsTracker tracker
        -AliasValidator validator
        +shorten(longUrl String) String
        +resolve(shortCode String) String
    }
    Base62Encoder ..|> UrlEncoder : implements
    CustomAliasEncoder --|> Base62Encoder : extends
    InMemoryStore ..|> CodeStore : implements
    RedisStore ..|> CodeStore : implements
    NoOpTracker ..|> AnalyticsTracker : implements
    DatabaseTracker ..|> AnalyticsTracker : implements
    CustomAliasValidator ..|> AliasValidator : implements
    UrlShortenerService o-- UrlEncoder : uses (injected)
    UrlShortenerService o-- CodeStore : uses (injected)
    UrlShortenerService o-- AnalyticsTracker : uses (injected)
    UrlShortenerService o-- AliasValidator : uses (injected)
```

**Observable outcome:** Any Spring @Bean that satisfies an interface can be wired in — production configs, test configs, and migration configs all swap implementations without modifying the service itself.

## End-to-end outcome

Approach A — Hashing (MD5/SHA): - Hash the long URL: MD5("https://...") = 3b94d2a8...

## Alternatives considered

### Decision Guide: Choosing the Right URL Shortener Architecture

Start with a single DB + auto-increment.


## Failure and degraded modes

### Trade-offs & Failure Modes: Custom Aliases and Collision Handling

- **Detection:** Users sometimes want custom codes: tiny.url/my-blog .
- **User or operator impact:** Users sometimes want custom codes: tiny.url/my-blog .

seriesList.name: Architecture Patterns for Production Systems
seriesList.description: High-level design is only half the battle; the other half is surviving production. This series explores the architectural patterns required to build resilient, scalable, and maintainable systems. We dive into the trade-offs of microservices vs. monoliths, event-driven architectures, caching strategies, and data consistency models. Each post focuses on proven patterns that solve common bottlenecks in high-traffic production environments, helping you move from "it works on my machine" to "it works at scale."

seriesList.name: Architecture Patterns for Production Systems
seriesList.description: High-level design is only half the battle; the other half is surviving production. This series explores the architectural patterns required to build resilient, scalable, and maintainable systems. We dive into the trade-offs of microservices vs. monoliths, event-driven architectures, caching strategies, and data consistency models. Each post focuses on proven patterns that solve common bottlenecks in high-traffic production environments, helping you move from "it works on my machine" to "it works at scale."

seriesList.name: Data Structures and Algorithms
seriesList.description: Master the core of computer science. This series demystifies Data Structures and Algorithms, from Big O to graph theory. Learn to write efficient, scalable code and ace your technical interviews with confidence.

seriesList.name: How It Works: Internals Explained
seriesList.description: Ever wondered what actually happens when you trigger a function, commit a transaction, or deploy a container? This series peels back the layers of abstraction to explore the low-level mechanics of modern technology. From database engines and operating system internals to the hidden plumbing of distributed systems, we dive deep into the source code and architectural designs that make complex software work. No magic, just engineering.

seriesList.name: Low-Level Design Guide
seriesList.description: Good architecture is built on a foundation of solid low-level design. This series is a deep dive into the "micro" side of software engineering—focusing on class design, object-oriented principles (SOLID), and tactical design patterns. We explore how to translate requirements into clean, maintainable code, handle concurrency at the component level, and define clear interfaces. Whether you're preparing for LLD interviews or looking to sharpen your day-to-day coding craftsmanship, this guide provides the blueprints for building modular software.

seriesList.name: Machine Learning Fundamentals
seriesList.description: This series breaks down complex mathematical theories and algorithms into simple, intuitive explanations with practical examples, making AI accessible to everyone from beginners to aspiring data scientists.

seriesList.name: Software Engineering Principles
seriesList.description: Writing code is easy; engineering software that lasts is hard. This series explores the core philosophies and mental models that define professional software development. We go beyond syntax to discuss the timeless principles of modularity, abstraction, testing strategies, and technical debt management. Whether we’re discussing the Zen of Python or the rigors of formal verification, this series provides a high-level perspective on how to think like an engineer, not just a coder.
